name: Ramus / vertical ramus augmentation

lead: The ramus is the vertical branch of the lower jaw rising from the jaw angle toward the ear. Augmenting it adds height there, usually with an implant, so the jawline looks longer and more defined from the side.

It is discussed mainly as one part of a custom wrap-around jaw implant design. The published medical literature on ramus implants concerns dental anchorage and jaw reconstruction; no study of ramus augmentation for appearance was found.

paras: People generally approach it as a component of a custom implant plan made with a surgeon, rather than a standalone item. The shape change shows after healing.
Risks have not been studied for the cosmetic use. General implant risks include infection, displacement and nerve injury near the jaw.

angle.text: A longer, squarer jawline from added height along the vertical jaw. An implant placed along the ramus raises the jaw angle, and the shape change is visible after healing. Very little cosmetic outcome data has been published.

lead: The mandibular ramus is the vertical portion of the lower jaw that connects the angle of the jaw to the joint near the ear. Ramus augmentation, or vertical ramus augmentation, refers to adding implant material along the ramus to increase its apparent height and the definition of the jaw angle. People pursue it to get a longer, squarer jawline in profile and a more defined line between the jaw and neck.[1]

Looksmaxxing communities discuss it mainly as one element of custom or wrap-around jaw implant designs, alongside chin and gonial-angle implants, and as a counterpart to the 'ramus' side of facial proportion discussions, where a long ramus is described as part of a strong lower face. Forum members also ask whether non-surgical habits can lengthen the ramus.[2][3] In the published literature, ramus implants address different questions: dental implants placed in the ramus area for denture support or orthodontic anchorage, and mechanical testing of implants used in jaw reconstruction.[4][5][6][7] No study was found examining ramus augmentation for cosmetic purposes.

Ramus height is also part of everyday facial-proportion talk: a taller ramus is described as giving a longer back-of-jaw line, and the angle between ramus and jaw body is discussed as a marker of a squarer or more rounded lower face. Wikipedia reports that the angle of the mandible is obtuse at birth, about 175 degrees, narrows to roughly 110 to 120 degrees in adults, and widens again to about 140 degrees in old age.[1]
infobox: Sagittal split ramus osteotomy, vertical ramus osteotomy, mandibular distraction

paras: The human mandible has a horseshoe-shaped body that carries the lower teeth and gives the chin its structure, and two rami that rise from the back of the body. Each ramus is a flat, four-sided plate whose outer surface gives attachment to the masseter muscle, while the inner surface carries the opening of the mandibular canal and the attachment of the medial pterygoid muscle.[1] The lower border of the ramus meets the back border at the angle of the mandible, which may be inverted or everted. At the top, the ramus ends in two processes, the coronoid in front and the condyle behind, the latter forming part of the temporomandibular joint.[1]

Because the ramus is the part of the jaw most visible from the side between the ear and the jaw angle, its height and the angle at which it meets the body shape the profile of the lower face. Face-shape discussions in looksmaxxing communities refer to this as ramus length or 'ramus height', and sometimes to counterclockwise or clockwise rotation of the jaw.

Wikipedia notes that the angle of the mandible is nearly square in adults, about 110 to 120 degrees, compared with about 175 degrees at birth, about 140 degrees by the fourth year of life, and about 140 degrees again in old age, when tooth loss and bone resorption make the ramus more oblique.[1] The ramus develops from Meckel's cartilage of the first pharyngeal arch.[1] The masseter attaches to the outer surface and the medial pterygoid to the inner surface, and the inferior alveolar nerve enters the mandibular foramen on the inner side and runs through the ramus in the mandibular canal.[1] These relationships explain why jaw contouring is discussed in terms of muscle function and lip and chin sensation.

Augmenting the ramus differs from widening the jaw at the angle: the goal is added vertical height along the back of the jaw, which affects the look of the jawline in profile. It is commonly mentioned together with chin and angle augmentation in custom jaw implant designs, where an implant is shaped to a patient's imaging and placed along the bone surface.

Surgeons also alter the ramus in other contexts that are not implants. Sagittal split ramus osteotomy is a standard step in orthognathic surgery to move the lower jaw, and a 2024 clinical study of 35 patients undergoing orthognathic procedures examined taste changes afterward.[8] Intraoral vertical ramus osteotomy, used to set the jaw back, has been studied for relapse after surgery.[9] A 2023 report described a ramus-angle switch and flip osteotomy.[10] Mandibular distraction osteogenesis is used to lengthen a deficient ramus and body in conditions such as Treacher Collins syndrome.[11] Reduction of the angle and ramus is part of jaw reduction surgery in facial feminization.[12] These procedures change the bone rather than add material and are not described as cosmetic ramus augmentation.

Interest in the ramus grew out of facial-proportion discussion on looksmax.org, where members ask what can be done about ramus length.[2][3] Threads titled simply 'Ramus' show the typical pattern: a member asks what can be done, and replies split between chewing-based 'mechanical tension' advice for people who are still growing and statements that real change requires surgery.[2][3] Members also bring in material from other sources, such as a T Nation thread that quotes a finding about growth hormone and craniofacial growth in children.[13]
Because published cosmetic ramus augmentation outcomes are not available, information on implant results circulates mainly as individual accounts rather than as studies.

Facial plastic surgery offers several routes to change the lower face. Jaw and chin implants add volume on the bone surface; Wikipedia's chin augmentation article lists silicone, porous polyethylene (Medpor), ePTFE and acellular dermal matrix as chin implant materials, with silicone described as easy to remove but able to shift or contribute to bone resorption, and polyethylene as allowing tissue ingrowth that anchors it but makes removal harder.[14][15] These descriptions concern chin implants; the article does not address mandibular angle or ramus implants specifically.[14]

Osteotomy-based surgery moves the patient's own bone. Wikipedia describes the bilateral sagittal split osteotomy, in which the surgeon cuts through the ramus, splits the mandible and repositions it, fixing it with titanium plates and screws; it describes healing of 2 to 6 weeks with full bony union taking another 2 to 4 months, and facial aesthetics and symmetry as recognised goals alongside bite correction.[16] The same article reports nerve injury, usually to the inferior alveolar nerve, as a known complication, often temporary and typically recovering within about three months, with permanent numbness described as rare and infection rates of up to 7 percent reported.[16] For chin contour, sliding genioplasty moves a segment of bone forward or back, and the Wikipedia article says bone-based correction is usually more dramatic than implants.[15]

Reduction procedures take the opposite direction: jaw reduction surgery reshapes the angle and ramus to narrow the lower face and is described in the facial feminization literature, along with masseter muscle reduction.[12][17] In children with Treacher Collins syndrome, which involves an underdeveloped lower jaw and in severe forms an absent or shortened ramus, mandibular distraction and mandibular advancement are used to lengthen the jaw, mainly for breathing and function, with appearance improved as a result.[11][18]

A 1971 report in a dental implantology journal described observations following use of a ramus implant, a device used for denture support rather than facial contour.[5] A 1992 French paper reported ten years of experience with a mandibular ramus implant framework,[6] and a 2011 Chinese study examined ramus implant anchorage for distalizing the lower dental arch in orthodontics.[7] Several patents from 1980 to 1994 describe dental ramus implants and denture support frames anchored in the lower jaw.[19] These are not cosmetic studies.

A 2016 cadaver and finite-element study evaluated how a commercial alloplastic implant fixed to a mandibular ramus transfers load after resection, which concerns reconstruction after tumor or trauma.[4] A registered phase 1/2 trial is evaluating a bioengineered bone graft for ramus reconstruction in patients with mandible tumors and injuries.[20] Grafts taken from the ramus are also used as a bone source for building up dental ridges.[21]

No study has measured complication rates for cosmetic ramus augmentation. Surgical literature on the jaw describes the mandibular canal running through the ramus and the inferior alveolar nerve entering it,[1] which is why jaw procedures are discussed in terms of altered lip and chin sensation; the 2024 orthognathic study above examined taste change, another nerve-related outcome.[8] For related facial implants, Wikipedia lists swelling, hematoma and temporary lip weakness or numbness as common and usually minor, and infection, bony changes, implant displacement and nerve damage as less common, noting that surgeon experience is a key factor.[14] Jaw procedures also carry general risks of surgery near the mouth, including infection.[16] On forums, members describe jaw surgery in general as carrying 'high complications'.[3]

No studies found on cosmetic vertical ramus augmentation. Studies of ramus implants in dentistry and reconstruction exist but address different purposes.[4][5][6][7] Related research includes a 2020 study of relapse after intraoral vertical ramus osteotomy,[9] a 2024 clinical study of taste change after orthognathic surgery,[8] a 2021 review of mandibular distraction in Treacher Collins syndrome[11] and a 2022 review of jaw reduction surgery.[12]

Related jaw-focused practices in looksmaxxing include chin and gonial-angle implants, masseter work, orthognathic surgery, mewing and chewing routines. Chewing-based claims about the ramus appear in forum threads but have not been tested in published studies.[2]
